MMA is a tamer version of a sport which was called pankration in the time of the Stoics. Pankration was arguably the most popular ancient Olympic sport, with wrestling and boxing close behind, and was a highly valued skill set. Alexander the Great kept in close company with accomplished pankratiasts and his armies quite likely spread the influence of pankration to the ancient Indian martial art vajra-musti, which in turn influenced the ancient Oriental martial arts, which in turn, many centuries later, came to influence modern Western MMA and military combatives. Though many see MMA as a modern phenomenon, it is in fact the continuation of a millennia-old tradition some say began with the legendary heroes Heracles and Theseus.

The early modern MMA fighters used to train a mix of martial arts, but these days mixed martial arts is an established martial discipline in its own right. There are plenty of very good MMA schools out there, but the popularity of the sport means there are also a lot of bad schools out there, too. Be sure to vet the quality and character of both the instructor and his students. If the MMA schools in your area don't seem like the kind of place you'd want to send yourself or your kids, consider checking into schools which teach the component arts.

For grappling, I would suggest wrestling, judo, and/or Brasilian jiu jitsu. For striking: boxing, kickboxing, and/or muay thai. Consider a heavier focus on grappling than striking, especially for your son. Wrestling kept me out of trouble in school in ways that boxing would not have: being able to subdue a minor troublemaker without injury has some value over resorting to dangerous blows (or joint locks) in a situation where the other guy isn't really dangerous and just needs a minute to cool down.

 

Other considerations for a comprehensive combatives package: gunfighting, Filipino Martial Arts, and parkour.

Gunfighting is self-explanatory and you can find competition circuits geared towards different aspects of that. Look up practical shooting, three-gun, and similar. Keep in mind that the way one moves for competition isn't necessarily the way one moves while getting shot at and address those differences, either in practice or with paintball, airsoft, or the like.

FMA (also called eskrima, kali, or arnis) is pretty much the modern gold standard for edged and improvised weapons when you find legitimate teachers--the evasive footwork of modern western boxing comes from the Philippines, where they train to avoid knives instead of soaking up hits from fists.

Parkour (not freerunning) is not one people generally think of as a martial art, but it is of a martial origin and application (it's the origin of the modern military obstacle course). Its utility is in escaping a bad situation or otherwise gaining a positional advantage efficiently. If you've ever seen a Jackie Chan movie, think about how he fights large groups: he doesn't stand there and fight them all at once, he runs away and uses objects and terrain to fight them one or two at a time. Being able to avoid and escape bad situations is arguably a more important ass-saving skill than being able to fight. The man considered its founder, Georges Hébert, has some worthwhile ideas on virtue and physical training (his personal motto: "Être fort pour être utile" ["Be strong to be useful"]) and the discipline itself changes the way one thinks about one's surroundings.
